candidates.speaker: Aron Ra
candidates.proposition: Treating naturalism as a positive denial of anything supernatural improperly shifts the burden of proof onto nonbelievers.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly gives Aron Ra the floor, and the uninterrupted opening statement follows.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This establishes the con side's governing interpretation of the motion and its central burden-of-proof objection.
candidates.contextSummary: Aron Ra opens by disputing the framing of naturalism as a truth-valued positive doctrine and compares that framing with burden shifting over atheism.

candidates.speaker: Aron Ra
candidates.proposition: Acceptance of the physical world does not itself establish the stronger claim that no immaterial or supernatural reality exists.
candidates.attributionBasis: The passage remains within Aron Ra's uninterrupted opening statement after his explicit introduction.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The distinction limits what the con side must defend and challenges an asserted equivalence among naturalism, physicalism, and materialism.
candidates.contextSummary: The speaker distinguishes ordinary realism about a material world from a positive exclusion of all supernatural alternatives and notes definitional ambiguity.

candidates.speaker: Aron Ra
candidates.proposition: Methodological naturalism is justified because scientific claims must rest on testable evidence, while supernatural claims have produced no reliable demonstrations.
candidates.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted opening statement and first-person argumentative framing identify Aron Ra as the speaker.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This supplies the con side's affirmative evidential rationale for naturalistic scientific practice and its rejection of supernatural explanations.
candidates.contextSummary: Aron Ra defines methodological naturalism through evidence, testing, and falsifiability, then argues that purported supernatural practitioners have shown no dependable success.

candidates.speaker: Aron Ra
candidates.proposition: Anyone seeking to refute naturalism must substantiate a supernatural alternative rather than require naturalists to prove an undefined negative.
candidates.attributionBasis: This is the closing portion of Aron Ra's opening, immediately before the moderator changes speakers.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move states the con side's proposed burden allocation and its direct standard for resolving the debate motion.
candidates.contextSummary: Aron Ra offers to consider legitimate evidence for supernatural reality but refuses to prove that no undefined immaterial alternative exists.

candidates.speaker: David Wood
candidates.proposition: Metaphysical naturalism claims that only the natural world is real and therefore carries a burden of proof in a debate over whether it is true.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly transfers the floor to David Wood, whose uninterrupted opening contains this passage.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This defines the proposition the pro side contests and directly rejects the con side's proposed refusal of a burden of proof.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Aron Ra's claim that he need not prove an undefined supernatural negative and may place the burden entirely on Wood

candidates.contextSummary: David Wood distinguishes metaphysical naturalism from methodological naturalism and argues that affirming the former in this debate requires supporting it.

candidates.speaker: David Wood
candidates.proposition: A method that automatically reinterprets every possible contrary observation can reject any position and is therefore not a rational evidential methodology.
candidates.attributionBasis: The passage occurs continuously within David Wood's moderator-introduced opening statement.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The argument challenges the skeptical evidential posture Wood associates with the con side and prepares his critique of naturalism's epistemic foundations.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Aron Ra's evidence-centered demand that Wood substantiate supernatural reality while Aron declines a positive defense of naturalism

candidates.contextSummary: Wood uses analogies involving flat-earth denial and proving another person's existence to argue that unrestricted skeptical reinterpretation defeats any evidence.

candidates.speaker: David Wood
candidates.proposition: Naturalism is catastrophically self-undermining because accepting its account of cognition removes rational warrant for trusting the cognition that affirms it.
candidates.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly pivots to naturalism during David Wood's uninterrupted opening statement.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This is the pro side's principal thesis and directly states the evolutionary-naturalist cognitive-reliability critique posed by the motion.
candidates.contextSummary: After illustrating self-undermining hypotheses with an omnipotent deceiver, Wood argues that naturalistically produced faculties were not made for judging naturalism.

candidates.speaker: David Wood
candidates.proposition: If beliefs result entirely from nonrational physical causes governed by natural laws rather than truth, naturalism supplies no basis for trusting those beliefs.
candidates.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted opening statement remains David Wood's, with no moderator or speaker transition.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This provides the causal mechanism for the central self-undermining argument by separating belief production from sensitivity to truth.
candidates.contextSummary: Wood characterizes cognition under naturalism as physical cause and effect, arguing that the same indifferent processes determine both true and false beliefs.

candidates.speaker: David Wood
candidates.proposition: Natural selection favors survival and reproduction rather than truth, so evolved faculties lack warrant when extended to abstract claims such as naturalism.
candidates.attributionBasis: This extended argument remains within David Wood's clearly introduced and uninterrupted opening statement.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move supplies the evolutionary component of the pro case and answers the anticipated claim that selection generally produces reliable cognition.
candidates.contextSummary: Wood argues that false beliefs can aid fitness, that selection rewards practical behavior, and that faculties shaped for basic tasks are unreliable in metaphysics.

candidates.speaker: Aron Ra
candidates.proposition: Human social evolution favored empathy, cooperation, trustworthiness, and widening concern, giving selection reasons to preserve dependable social cognition.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly begins Aron Ra's rebuttal, and this passage continues without a speaker change.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This is the con side's first direct evolutionary answer to the claim that selection rewards only selfish fitness rather than dependable cognition and conduct.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: David Wood's argument that natural selection targets mere survival and reproduction without favoring reliable truth-directed cognitive faculties

candidates.contextSummary: Aron Ra argues that humans survived through group solidarity and empathy, while persistently selfish or unreliable individuals were socially excluded across generations.

candidates.speaker: Aron Ra
candidates.proposition: Naturalists need not prove a negative when supernaturalists have not supplied evidence for any supernatural aspect of reality.
candidates.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted first-person response addresses Mr. Wood by name and continues until a clear transition to another example.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This directly contests where the burden lies in a debate over naturalism and challenges the claim that withholding supernatural belief is irrational.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Wood's demand that the naturalist defend naturalism and his characterization of naturalistic confidence as irrational.

candidates.contextSummary: After completing an evolutionary account of social morality, Aron turns to Wood's supernatural skepticism standard, burden allocation, and cognitive-reliability criticism.

candidates.speaker: Aron Ra
candidates.proposition: An affirmative atheist position can be defended because there is evidence against souls and major scriptural supernatural claims, not merely an absence of supporting evidence.
candidates.attributionBasis: Aron explicitly identifies his own progression from agnostic atheism to an affirmative belief and states that he will defend it rationally.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move answers the demand for an affirmative case and supplies a claimed evidential basis for rejecting central supernatural propositions.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Wood's contention that Aron avoids defending an affirmative worldview while placing the entire burden on supernaturalists.

candidates.contextSummary: Following examples of belief-shaped religious experiences, Aron distinguishes lack-of-belief atheism from his stronger position and claims counterevidence to supernatural doctrines.

candidates.speaker: David Wood
candidates.proposition: If naturalism makes every assertion the causally determined product of particles in motion, naturalists lack a rational basis for taking either participant's assertions seriously.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator hands the floor to David, who immediately identifies Aron's prior remarks and develops the particles-in-motion objection in one continuous turn.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This states the core cognitive-reliability critique by arguing that a naturalistic causal origin of belief undercuts rational confidence in the resulting worldview.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Aron's preceding evidential and experiential defense of naturalism and his claim to reason rationally from the available evidence.

candidates.contextSummary: David begins his response by reframing everything Aron said as naturalistically determined physical output, then invokes Darwin's doubt about higher convictions.

candidates.speaker: David Wood
candidates.proposition: Evolutionary explanations for empathy and cooperative herd behavior do not establish reliable cognitive faculties for discovering comprehensive truths about the universe.
candidates.attributionBasis: David explicitly summarizes Aron's evolutionary account of ethics, concedes its population-mechanics claims, and identifies the inference he disputes.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The reply separates the adaptive value of social behavior from truth-tracking on grand worldview questions, preserving the critique against Aron's evolutionary explanation.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Aron's account of empathy, cooperation, ostracism, and morality as products of evolutionary population mechanics.

candidates.contextSummary: David grants that concern for fellow group members can aid survival but denies that this provides grounds for trusting cognition about naturalism or cosmic truth.

candidates.speaker: David Wood
candidates.proposition: Evolutionary naturalism generates several defeaters for worldview belief, including causal determinism, epiphenomenal mental states, and selection for survival rather than cosmic truth.
candidates.attributionBasis: The same identified speaker develops a connected sequence of naturalism-specific cognitive objections without interruption until shifting to Aron's flat-earth example.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This is the most developed statement of the affirmative case, specifying multiple mechanisms by which naturalism allegedly undermines confidence in naturalistic conclusions.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Aron's claim that Wood mistakenly attributes cognitive self-undermining to evolution and fails to understand evolutionary mechanics.

candidates.contextSummary: David distinguishes evolution alone from evolution combined with naturalism, then explains determinism, Huxley's train-whistle analogy, and survival-selected faculties.

candidates.speaker: David Wood
candidates.proposition: A naturalism that can reinterpret every conceivable apparent manifestation of God as aliens or another natural cause becomes insulated from contrary evidence and is not a good-faith evidential position.
candidates.attributionBasis: David explicitly takes up Aron's good-faith criterion and develops the Dawkins, powerful-alien, Shermer, and Atkins examples as a continuous rebuttal.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move challenges the falsifiability and evidential openness of the opposing worldview, supporting the claim that demands for supernatural evidence may be impossible to satisfy.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Aron's claim that empirical propositions can be proved to sincere interlocutors and that good-faith evidential engagement is the key distinction.

candidates.contextSummary: David agrees that good- and bad-faith discussions differ, then argues that prominent naturalists precommit to natural reinterpretations of any apparent divine evidence.

candidates.speaker: Aron Ra
candidates.proposition: Because both sides accept the known natural world, the person adding a supernatural realm bears the burden of justifying that addition through independent, repeatable, objective verification.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator gives Aron the rebuttal, and Aron directly contrasts the shared natural world with Wood's additional supernatural assumption throughout the window.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This supplies the con side's central burden-of-proof framework and states the empirical conditions under which a supernatural addition could become justified.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Wood's argument that naturalism itself requires defense and that naturalists are committed to rejecting any possible supernatural evidence.

candidates.contextSummary: Aron rejects the proposed burden shift, says Wood offered no supernatural evidence, and describes regular, independent, testable confirmation as the appropriate standard.

candidates.speaker: David Wood
candidates.proposition: Metaphysical naturalism resembles solipsism because it can reinterpret every possible challenge within its own framework, yet its adherents still avoid defending their comprehensive position while trusting unreliable cognition.
candidates.attributionBasis: After the moderator gives David four minutes, David announces an analogy and develops it continuously from solipsism through burden allocation and cognitive reliability.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The analogy unifies the affirmative challenges concerning burden of proof, insulation from rebuttal, and confidence in faculties whose reliability naturalism allegedly compromises.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Aron's refusal to accept the burden for naturalism and his appeal to personal investigation as support for rejecting supernatural claims.

candidates.contextSummary: David compares naturalism with an unfalsifiable solipsistic worldview, argues that holding a comprehensive metaphysics carries a burden, and closes with the charge of faith.

candidates.speaker: David Wood
candidates.proposition: Aron's personal skeptical experience cannot justify dismissing vast numbers of reported miracles, especially if naturalism already gives him reason to doubt the reliability of his own cognitive faculties.
candidates.attributionBasis: David takes over after Aron's short reply and directly contrasts Aron's experiences with other reported experiences before returning to the cognitive-reliability objection.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This applies the affirmative reliability critique to Aron's evidential judgments and challenges the scope of the inference from his personal debunking experiences to others' reports.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Aron's distinction between deceptive subjective experience and failed objective verification of his former supernatural beliefs.

candidates.contextSummary: David argues that others report contrary experiences, extrapolates from a survey of miracle reports, and says Aron claims excessive certainty despite naturalistic cognitive limits.

candidates.speaker: Aron Ra
candidates.proposition: Repeated objective failure of supernatural claims, together with explicit conditions that would change his mind, supports naturalism without claiming omniscience or insulating it from evidence.
candidates.attributionBasis: Aron expressly denies David's characterization and gives a continuous first-person account of failed verification and his evidential conditions through the end of the core.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move directly answers the alleged self-defeat and unfalsifiability of naturalism by grounding confidence in repeated testing and specifying potentially disconfirming evidence.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Wood's charge that Aron dismisses widespread miracle testimony through an unreliable naturalistic faculty amounting to near-omniscience.

candidates.contextSummary: Aron denies making the attributed claim, cites the collapse of previously accepted paranormal evidence, accepts a burden to state standards, and asks Wood for positive verification.

candidates.speaker: Aron Ra
candidates.proposition: Naturalism should be evaluated objectively, and rejecting it requires demonstrating some supernatural addition rather than merely criticizing a participant's beliefs.
candidates.attributionBasis: The turn directly continues Aron Ra's first-person defense and is followed by Wood questioning whether his thoughts are physically determined.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move states Aron's central burden-of-proof account for the motion and challenges Wood to identify an objectively demonstrable supernatural alternative.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Wood's earlier cognitive-reliability critique and characterization of Aron's naturalist position.

candidates.contextSummary: After disputing Wood's description of his beliefs, Aron distinguishes the debate's objective question from his personal history and demands evidence of anything beyond nature.

candidates.speaker: David Wood
candidates.proposition: A defender cannot establish a worldview merely by demanding that opponents disprove it, as illustrated by an analogous defense of metaphysical solipsism.
candidates.attributionBasis: The speaker introduces Wood's solipsism analogy immediately after Aron's burden challenge, and Aron responds by rejecting that hypothetical debate.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The analogy directly contests Aron's allocation of the burden of proof and supports Wood's claim that naturalism itself requires a positive rational defense.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Aron's claim that Wood must disprove naturalism by showing that something supernatural exists.

candidates.contextSummary: Wood compares Aron's defense of naturalism with a solipsist who treats the failure to prove an external world as sufficient support for solipsism.

candidates.speaker: Aron Ra
candidates.proposition: Whether framed as asserting only nature or merely acknowledging the known natural world, Wood still bears the burden of showing that something beyond nature exists.
candidates.attributionBasis: The speaker rejects Wood's hypothetical and repeatedly states Aron's adopted position and demand that Wood demonstrate a supernatural aspect.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This is Aron's principal procedural and substantive answer: naturalism remains warranted absent a demonstrated supernatural exception to the observed natural world.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Wood's metaphysical-solipsism analogy and claim that naturalism needs its own positive case.

candidates.contextSummary: Aron dismisses the analogy as a different debate, accepts the stated naturalist position for purposes of this debate, and reiterates Wood's evidential burden.

candidates.speaker: David Wood
candidates.proposition: Naturalism can be rejected without proving supernaturalism because its account of nonrational causes and survival-oriented cognition makes confident affirmation of the worldview incoherent.
candidates.attributionBasis: Wood explicitly identifies his philosophical response, defines metaphysical naturalism, and develops the omnipotent-deceiver and cognitive-faculty analogies.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move presents the debate's core cognitive-reliability critique and explains why internal incoherence alone could defeat rational confidence in naturalism.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Aron's contention that the only relevant route to rejecting naturalism is demonstrating a supernatural reality.

candidates.contextSummary: Wood argues that a worldview may be defeated internally, then claims naturalism gives cognition only nonrational, survival-directed origins unsuited to judging all reality.

candidates.speaker: Aron Ra
candidates.proposition: Humans must provisionally accept sensory experience as reality, and Wood's skepticism does not relieve him of showing an exception to the natural world.
candidates.attributionBasis: The speaker invokes Hume's claim that humans have no choice but to trust perception, then restates Aron's two formulations of the evidential burden.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move answers the global skepticism argument while preserving Aron's core contention that Wood must supply evidence for something beyond the natural world.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Wood's claim that naturalism undermines trust in faculties used to affirm naturalism or assess reality.

candidates.contextSummary: Aron answers that ordinary reliance on perception is unavoidable and argues that under either naturalist formulation Wood still must demonstrate something else exists.

candidates.speaker: David Wood
candidates.proposition: Humean and Darwinian doubts about the reach of human cognition show that one can withhold affirmation of naturalism without affirming any supernatural alternative.
candidates.attributionBasis: Wood names Hume and Darwin, attributes skeptical conclusions to them, and expressly distinguishes rejecting naturalism from proving supernaturalism.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move supplies historical examples for Wood's central distinction between withholding rational confidence in naturalism and positively defending supernaturalism.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Aron's insistence that rejecting naturalism requires evidence for a supernatural alternative.

candidates.contextSummary: Wood argues that Hume and Darwin would question their competence to judge ultimate reality, making agnosticism about naturalism a coherent outcome without supernatural commitment.

candidates.speaker: Aron Ra
candidates.proposition: Objective data rather than authorities or personal experiences should govern belief, and Wood has not supplied objective verification of anything supernatural.
candidates.attributionBasis: The first-person account of formerly trusting personal experience and demanding objective verification is characteristic of Aron's stated evidential position throughout the exchange.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move condenses Aron's epistemic standard and directly contrasts publicly verifiable data with both testimonial experience and Wood's cognitive skepticism.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Wood's appeal to Darwin, Hume, Dawkins, and doubts about naturalistically produced cognitive faculties.

candidates.contextSummary: Aron denies treating Dawkins as an authority, says personal experiences proved unreliable, and maintains that Wood has not met the requested objective evidential standard.

candidates.speaker: David Wood
candidates.proposition: If beliefs result from causally determined particles, epiphenomenal mental states, and faculties selected only for survival, naturalists lack grounds for trusting those faculties about ultimate reality.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator hands the closing statement to David, who explicitly recaps his opening argument and develops determinism, epiphenomenalism, and evolutionary selection.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This closing synthesis states the pro side's complete cognitive-reliability case and applies it directly to the rational affirmation of naturalism.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Aron's reliance on objective data and his denial that natural origins make human reasoning irrational.

candidates.contextSummary: Wood argues that deterministic physical causes, causally idle mental states, and survival-selected faculties cannot justify sweeping judgments about reality or naturalism itself.

candidates.speaker: Aron Ra
candidates.proposition: Emergent bottom-up processes explain apparent design, while supernatural and religious claims remain unverified or falsified and must establish possibility before probability or fact.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator gives Aron the closing statement, and the speaker reiterates Aron's emergence argument and longstanding critique of supernatural evidence.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The closing integrates Aron's naturalistic explanation of apparent design with his evidential case that supernatural alternatives have not cleared even the threshold of possibility.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Wood's closing claim that naturalistic emergence and evolved cognition cannot support rational confidence.

candidates.contextSummary: Aron rejects Wood's characterization, presents design as an emergent bottom-up appearance, and argues that religious, miraculous, and other supernatural claims consistently lack verification.

candidates.speaker: David Wood
candidates.proposition: A supernatural event would leave natural effects that remain open to natural reinterpretation, so identifying it depends on evidential patterns rather than a simple measuring device.
candidates.attributionBasis: An audience member addresses David, after which Wood answers in the first person and uses a miraculous cancer-healing example before Aron begins disagreeing.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The answer addresses the central verification challenge by explaining why supernatural causation may not be directly measurable even when its resulting physical effects are observable.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: The audience question asking for a consistent method of measuring a supernatural or non-natural world.

candidates.contextSummary: Wood concedes that he lacks a consistent supernatural measurement procedure, then argues that miraculous effects become ordinary physical facts susceptible to alternative natural explanations.

candidates.speaker: Aron Ra
candidates.proposition: If purported magic or miracles consistently produced observable effects that defied physical explanation, they would constitute discoverable evidence of the supernatural.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly passes the discussion to the other debater, whose first-person account and skeptical position identify Aron Ra.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move supplies the naturalist side's evidential criterion for supernatural claims and explains why the absence of reproducible examples matters.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: David Wood's claim that supernatural occurrences would become naturally describable immediately after occurring.

candidates.contextSummary: After Wood says supernatural intervention could always be redescribed naturally, Aron distinguishes lawful observable magic from unsupported claims and reports finding no evidence for it.

candidates.speaker: Aron Ra
candidates.proposition: Religious prophecies commonly reflect retrospective revision, and the few verifiably prior predictions can fail rather than establish supernatural knowledge.
candidates.attributionBasis: The skeptical response follows an audience member's prophecy examples and uses Aron's characteristic comparative discussion of religious claims.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This move directly contests prophecy as independent evidence for supernaturalism by offering a general alternative explanation and a claimed counterexample.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: The audience claim that Zoroastrian and biblical predictions were fulfilled and therefore indicate supernatural involvement.

candidates.contextSummary: An audience member cites pre-Christian and biblical predictions; Aron cautions that popular prophecy parallels often cannot be verified and argues that retrospective fitting is widespread.

candidates.speaker: David Wood
candidates.proposition: Belief in supernatural reality does not require accepting every miracle report, because individual reports can range from weak or naturalistically explicable to genuinely suggestive.
candidates.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly announces a theistic perspective and contrasts his reactions with Aron's, clearly identifying David Wood.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move protects the cognitive-reliability critique from depending on indiscriminate credulity and articulates a discriminating approach to miracle testimony.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: The prophecy discussion and the broader skeptical suggestion that failed or dubious religious claims discredit supernatural belief.

candidates.contextSummary: Following Aron's criticism of prophecy claims, Wood separates general supernatural belief from acceptance of particular reports and describes assessing cases according to their evidential strength.

candidates.speaker: David Wood
candidates.proposition: Naturalism supplies cognitive faculties shaped for survival while treating them as reliable for conclusions far beyond verification, creating tension within the worldview itself.
candidates.attributionBasis: The response restates the cognitive-faculty argument advanced by David throughout the debate and directly answers the naturalist questioner.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This is a compact restatement of the debate's central pro contention that evolutionary naturalism undermines confidence in the reasoning used to affirm naturalism.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: The questioner's claim that collaborative confirmation handles cognitive limitations and challenge to treating rationality as supernatural.

candidates.contextSummary: A naturalist questioner points to measurable cognitive error and collaborative checking; Wood replies that the problem concerns confidence beyond verification given naturalism's own account of cognition.

candidates.speaker: Aron Ra
candidates.proposition: A documented apparent healing should be considered rather than dismissed, but prior experience with misrepresented supporting literature justifies initial doubt pending examination.
candidates.attributionBasis: The answer expresses Aron's evidence-first skepticism and refers to his recurring experience debating creationists and checking their cited papers.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The response defines the con side's stated openness to contrary evidence while explaining why extraordinary testimonial claims do not presently overturn naturalism.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: The audience member's medically documented vocal-cord recovery offered as a potentially compelling miracle case.

candidates.proposition: Rejecting naturalism for self-undermining incoherence does not establish supernaturalism; it can instead warrant withholding affirmation of either worldview.
candidates.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly distinguishes his personal theism from the narrower debate thesis, matching David Wood's stated argumentative burden.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move clarifies the pro side's burden and central conclusion: the argument seeks suspension of confidence in naturalism rather than direct proof of the supernatural.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: The audience questioner's characterization of David as asserting that reality contains more than the natural world.

candidates.contextSummary: When an audience member treats Wood as asserting supernatural reality, Wood separates his personal beliefs from the debate argument and says naturalism may be rejected without affirming its opposite.

candidates.proposition: Naturalistic cognition is either causally determined or affected by randomness, neither of which adds rational control, whereas theism can ground cognition in a truth-directed purpose.
candidates.attributionBasis: The answer contrasts naturalism with creation in God's image and follows a question directed against David's treatment of determinism.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This move defends the proposed link between naturalism and unreliable cognition while presenting the theistic account as capable of supplying a truth-oriented source.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: The audience objection that determinism need not follow from naturalism and would be experientially indistinguishable from free will.

candidates.speaker: David Wood
candidates.proposition: A deliberately rational machine could be trusted because of its programming, but evolved humans are selected for survival and reproduction rather than reliable grand metaphysical theorizing.
candidates.attributionBasis: The response answers a question explicitly addressed to David and reiterates his distinction between designed programming and evolved survival functions.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The machine analogy sharpens the principal pro argument by locating the reliability deficit not in determinism alone but in the evolutionary purpose assigned to cognition.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: The audience challenge that a fully deterministic machine programmed to reason rationally could still be considered reliable.

candidates.contextSummary: Asked why determinism would make a rational machine unreliable, Wood grants reliability under rational programming but denies that naturalism gives human cognition an analogous truth-directed function.

candidates.speaker: Aron Ra
candidates.proposition: Wood's descriptions of determinism and rationality do not match the naturalist account being defended, so the alleged incompatibility between naturalism and rational thought is unsupported.
candidates.attributionBasis: The first-person response rejects Wood's definitions from the naturalist side and is followed by Wood directly clarifying his determinism claim.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move attacks a key premise of the cognitive-reliability critique by disputing the conceptual account used to connect naturalism, determinism, and irrationality.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: David Wood's argument that survival-oriented deterministic cognition cannot reliably support a comprehensive theory such as naturalism.

candidates.contextSummary: Aron acknowledges limited formal philosophy study but maintains that neither reality nor rationality fits Wood's descriptions and that the claimed failure of naturalist rationality does not follow.

candidates.attributionBasis: The speaker conditionally retracts his own determinism point in response to Aron's objection, identifying David as the source of this qualification.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Aron Ra's objection that determinism is not an accurate or necessary description of naturalistic reality and rationality.
